title: Egypt
lead: The great kingdom of the Nile, which in the Bible is both refuge and prison: Abraham, Jacob's family and the infant Jesus find shelter there in hard times, but Israel is enslaved there and rescued in the exodus. Prophets warn against trusting Egypt and also foresee its conversion (Isaiah 19:19–25).

sections.b: Egypt appears from Abraham's journey in famine (Genesis 12:10–20) to Joseph's rule (Genesis 37–50), the slavery and exodus (Exodus 1–15), and Solomon's marriage alliance (1 Kings 3:1). Pharaoh Shishak (Shoshenq I) plundered Jerusalem after Solomon's death (1 Kings 14:25–26), and Pharaoh Neco killed King Josiah at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29). The prophets warn Judah against trusting Pharaoh (Isaiah 30:1–3; 31:1), threaten Israel with a "return to Egypt" as judgment (Hosea 8:13; 11:5), and pronounce long oracles against Egypt (Jeremiah 46; Ezekiel 29–32). Jeremiah was taken there by refugees (Jeremiah 43). Yet Isaiah foresees an altar to the LORD in Egypt and the blessing "Egypt my people" (Isaiah 19:19–25).
sections.refs: Genesis 12:10–20; Genesis 46:3–4; Exodus 1:8–14; Exodus 14:1–31; 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 14:25–26; 2 Kings 23:29; Isaiah 30:1–3; Isaiah 31:1; Hosea 8:13; Hosea 11:5; Jeremiah 46:1–28; Ezekiel 29:1–16; Jeremiah 43:1–7; Isaiah 19:19–25

sections.b: Joseph and Mary flee there with Jesus, and Matthew applies Hosea 11:1, "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Matthew 2:13–15). Stephen retells the stories of Joseph and Moses in Egypt (Acts 7:9–40), and Hebrews praises Moses for choosing disgrace with God's people over "the treasures of Egypt" (Hebrews 11:26). In Revelation, the city where the two witnesses die is "symbolically called Sodom and Egypt" (Revelation 11:8), making Egypt a symbol of oppression.
